lessons.title: From brooding to grow-out
lessons.html:
Managing the growing broiler

Post-brooding is the period after the first one to two weeks, when chicks no longer need supplementary heat for most of the day and the flock grows rapidly to slaughter weight, usually at about five to six weeks. Growth is fast, so small management mistakes quickly cost money. The supervisor manages environment, feed, water, health and staff so that the flock reaches target weight with low mortality and good feed conversion. Use the breeder company's management guide for target weights, temperatures and space.

Transition from brooding

  • Reduce temperature gradually as birds grow, following the guide and watching bird behaviour.
  • Expand the brooding area to the full house in steps, so birds are not crowded.
  • Remove chick feeder trays and paper and switch to the main feeder and drinker lines, at the correct height.
  • Change from starter to grower ration on schedule.

Equipment height and space

Raise feeders and drinkers as birds grow. Feeder pans should be at about the height of the birds' back; nipple drinkers should be set so birds stretch slightly to drink, as the guide describes. Check that each bird has enough feeder and drinker space for the stocking density.

Stocking density

Density is usually managed in kilograms of live weight per square metre at the end of the cycle. Overcrowding causes heat stress, poor litter, leg problems and higher mortality. Plan placement numbers according to house type, ventilation and the farm's welfare standards.

Record each change you make, with date and reason, on the house sheet.

lessons.title: Environment, feed and water
lessons.html:
The four essentials: air, temperature, feed and water

Ventilation and temperature

Growing broilers produce a lot of heat, moisture and carbon dioxide. Ventilation removes these and brings in fresh air.

  • Minimum ventilation in cool weather removes moisture and gases without chilling birds.
  • Transitional and tunnel ventilation in hot weather increases air speed over birds for cooling.
  • Evaporative cooling pads or foggers reduce temperature in South African summers; manage them carefully to avoid wet litter.

Watch the birds: panting and wings held out mean too hot; huddling means too cold; birds avoiding an area may mean draughts. A strong ammonia smell that makes your eyes water means ventilation is too low.

Litter

Keep litter dry and friable. Wet litter causes foot pad lesions, breast blisters, ammonia and disease. Fix leaking drinkers, adjust ventilation and remove caked litter where needed.

Feed

  • Feed phases such as grower and finisher are changed by age or weight on the feed programme.
  • Keep feed available and fresh; avoid feeder lines running empty.
  • Check feed deliveries for the correct ration, and record the quantity.
  • Withdrawal feed is used before slaughter if any medicated feed has been given, as the vet and label direct.

Water

Water intake rises sharply as birds grow and in hot weather. Record daily water intake from the meter. A sudden drop in water intake is often the first sign of a problem: disease, a blocked line or feed issues. Flush lines regularly and keep water clean and cool.

Lighting

Follow the lighting programme in the guide and the farm's welfare standards, which usually include a period of darkness every day for rest.

lessons.title: Monitoring performance and preparing for slaughter
lessons.html:
Measuring, recording and finishing the cycle

Weekly weighing

Weigh a random sample of birds from different parts of the house weekly. Compare with the target. Calculate uniformity. Poor growth or uniformity points to feeder or water access problems, disease, poor chick quality or environment problems.

Key performance figures

MeasureMeaning
Mortality %Birds dead and culled as a share of birds placed
Average live weightKilograms per bird at a given age
Feed conversion ratio (FCR)Kilograms of feed used per kilogram of live weight produced
Average daily gainGrams gained per bird per day
Production efficiency factorA combined index used by many integrators

Example: 60 000 kg of feed producing 36 000 kg of live weight gives an FCR of 60 000 ÷ 36 000 = 1,67.

Health and welfare

Walk the house at least twice a day. Cull sick and injured birds humanely through trained staff. Follow the vet's vaccination and treatment programme and record withdrawal periods. Report unusual mortality immediately; avian influenza and Newcastle disease are controlled diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Preparing for catching

  • Confirm the slaughter date and bird numbers with the abattoir.
  • Check withdrawal periods of any medicines are complete.
  • Withdraw feed for the time the abattoir specifies, but keep water available until catching.
  • Catch in dim light and in the cool part of the day, handle birds gently and do not overload crates.
  • Raise feeder and drinker lines to give catchers space.

Key points

  • Expand space, reduce temperature and raise equipment as birds grow, following the breed guide.
  • Ventilation removes heat, moisture and ammonia; watch bird behaviour.
  • Record daily water intake; a sudden drop is an early warning sign.
  • FCR = feed used ÷ live weight produced; track mortality and weight weekly.
  • Before catching, complete withdrawal periods, withdraw feed as specified and handle birds gently.
